researcher: researcher 3 (yardsticks: hazard labels, reference values with averaging times, odour thresholds)
question: For each candidate chemical, what is its cancer hazard label, which reference values exist and over what averaging time, and at what level can it (or petrol vapour, or diluted petrol exhaust) be smelled?
rulesForUse: A cancer classification is a hazard label (strength of evidence that something CAN cause cancer), not a risk from one red light. Never say or imply one red light causes cancer; never compute a cancer risk for one red light; never rank chemicals by harm.
Unit risks (WHO, EPA, OEHHA) are lifetime figures recorded for completeness only; they must not be applied to seconds or minutes of exposure.

Compare a red-light level only with a reference value of matching averaging time, after converting the red-light series to that averaging time. Where none exists, say so: no above/below statement can be made.
AEGLs are emergency-planning values for rare accidental releases; workplace limits are for healthy adult workers. Neither is a yardstick for everyday public air; if quoted, label them as such.
Carbon monoxide has no smell; particles are too small to see. Benzo[a]pyrene is particle-bound and has no smell of its own.

iarcGroupMeanings.Group 1: Carcinogenic to humans: there is convincing evidence that it can cause cancer in people.
iarcGroupMeanings.Group 2A: Probably carcinogenic to humans: limited evidence in people plus sufficient evidence in animals or strong mechanistic evidence.
iarcGroupMeanings.Group 2B: Possibly carcinogenic to humans: only one line of evidence (limited in people, or sufficient in animals, or strong mechanistic).
iarcGroupMeanings.Group 3: Not classifiable: evidence inadequate or limited; not a finding of safety.
iarcGroupMeanings.all: Each group is a hazard label (strength of evidence that the agent CAN cause cancer), not the risk at any exposure level (IARC Q&A).

conversions.basis: ug/m3 = ppm x molecular weight / 24.45 x 1000 (25 C, 1 atm)

noShortTermValue.statement: For a red light lasting seconds to about two minutes, no reference value of matching averaging time exists for ANY candidate chemical outside emergency (AEGL, 10-minute) and workplace (15-minute) limits. The shortest everyday-air values are 30 minutes (WHO: formaldehyde 100 ug/m3; odour guidelines for toluene 1 mg/m3 and styrene 70 ug/m3) and 1 hour (OEHHA acute RELs; Taiwan indoor formaldehyde 0.08 ppm and TVOC 0.56 ppm). A red-light peak can only be set beside these after converting to that averaging time (e.g. 1-hour mean = sum of concentration x seconds over the hour / 3600 s, with the rest of the hour at background), never as a raw 1-s or 10-s value.

odourSolidity.singleChemicals: Nagata 2003 is a standard single-laboratory compilation (triangle odour bag, 50% detection); repeat tests varied up to about 5-fold, and published compilations for the same chemical often differ by 10-fold or more (e.g. formaldehyde: Nagata 0.50 ppm vs WHO 2000 range 0.024-0.49 ppm). Treat any 'above odour threshold' for one chemical as order-of-magnitude.
odourSolidity.petrolVapour: API 1995: 0.47-0.58 ppm detection, three US fuel blends, one laboratory; abstract only. This is evaporated fuel, not exhaust.
odourSolidity.exhaust: Both exhaust figures come from English abstracts of 1960s-1970 European car-engine studies (Fiala 1967: 800-1,000-fold, four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine; BIL-32 1970: 10^3.72-10^3.83 = about 5,200-6,800-fold, petrol engines with control devices, idle and ECE cycle similar). The originals could not be opened. No measurement of odour concentration in scooter or motorcycle exhaust was found. The simulation's 6,800 is the top of the BIL-32 range (its low end is about 5,200), and 800 is the low end of Fiala's 800-1,000. Fiala found odour did not follow CO or HC (adding air lowered both but raised odour). Solidity: low. Supports 'smellable after roughly a thousand- to several-thousand-fold dilution', not an exact odour-unit number.
